stem: Two monosaccharide units in a disaccharide are joined by a
explanation: A condensation reaction between hydroxyl groups of two sugars forms a glycosidic bond and releases one water molecule. Peptide bonds join amino acids, ester bonds join fatty acids to glycerol and phosphodiester bonds link nucleotides.

stem: Complete hydrolysis of sucrose gives
explanation: Sucrose (cane sugar) is a disaccharide of one glucose and one fructose unit. Glucose plus galactose is lactose, and two glucose units make maltose, which are the usual confusions.

stem: The high specific heat capacity of water, which keeps body temperature stable, is mainly due to
options: strong covalent bonds within each molecule
its ionisation into H⁺ and OH⁻ ions
explanation: Much of the heat supplied to water is used to break hydrogen bonds between neighbouring polar molecules before the molecules can move faster, so temperature rises slowly. The O-H covalent bonds inside the molecule are not broken on heating, so they do not explain the effect.

stem: Cellulose differs from starch because cellulose is a polymer of
options: α-glucose joined by α-1,4 glycosidic bonds
β-glucose joined by β-1,4 glycosidic bonds
explanation: Cellulose is an unbranched chain of β-glucose with β-1,4 links, which lets chains lie side by side and form strong microfibrils. Starch (amylose and amylopectin) is built from α-glucose, with α-1,6 branches only in amylopectin.

stem: A peptide bond is formed between
options: the R groups of two neighbouring amino acids
the amino groups of two amino acids
the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of another
the carboxyl groups of two amino acids
explanation: In condensation, the -COOH of one amino acid reacts with the -NH₂ of the next, releasing water and forming the -CO-NH- peptide link. R groups do not take part in forming the backbone bond.

stem: A single polypeptide chain of 50 amino acids is made by condensation. The number of water molecules released is
explanation: Each peptide bond releases one water molecule, and a linear chain of n amino acids has n − 1 peptide bonds, so 50 − 1 = 49. Choosing 50 counts one bond per amino acid, forgetting that the two ends are free.

stem: The quaternary structure of a protein refers to
options: the sequence of amino acids in a chain
the association of two or more polypeptide chains
the coiling of a chain into an α-helix
the folding of a single chain into a compact 3-D shape
explanation: Quaternary structure exists only when a protein has more than one polypeptide, as in haemoglobin with four chains. The amino acid sequence is primary structure, α-helix is secondary and the 3-D folding of one chain is tertiary.

stem: A triglyceride is formed when glycerol combines with
options: one fatty acid and two phosphates
explanation: The three -OH groups of glycerol each form an ester bond with one fatty acid, releasing three water molecules. A phosphate group replaces one fatty acid only in a phospholipid, not in a triglyceride.

stem: In a phospholipid molecule, the part that is hydrophilic is the
explanation: The charged phosphate group (often with choline) attracts water, while the two non-polar fatty acid tails repel it. This is why phospholipids form a bilayer with heads facing the watery sides and tails inside.

stem: A sample of double-stranded DNA contains 18 % guanine. The percentage of adenine in it is
explanation: By base pairing G = C = 18 %, so G + C = 36 % and A + T = 64 %; since A = T, adenine = 32 %. 64 % is A + T together, not adenine alone.

stem: Which of the following is found in RNA but not in DNA?
explanation: RNA contains uracil in place of thymine and ribose in place of deoxyribose. Adenine occurs in both nucleic acids, while thymine and deoxyribose are features of DNA.

stem: Which pair of nitrogenous bases are both purines?
explanation: Purines (adenine and guanine) have a double ring, while pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine, uracil) have a single ring. Adenine-thymine and guanine-cytosine are complementary pairs, each made of one purine and one pyrimidine.

stem: A conjugated molecule formed by the combination of a protein with a carbohydrate is a
explanation: Glyco- refers to sugar, so a protein with a carbohydrate chain attached is a glycoprotein, common on cell surfaces. Lipoproteins carry lipid, nucleoproteins combine protein with nucleic acid, and a phospholipid contains no protein.

stem: The lock-and-key model of enzyme action was proposed by
explanation: Emil Fischer (1894) suggested that the active site has a rigid shape exactly matching the substrate, like a key in a lock. Koshland later proposed the induced-fit model, in which the active site changes shape slightly when the substrate binds.

stem: According to the induced-fit model of enzyme action,
options: the active site changes shape slightly as the substrate binds
the active site is rigid and exactly fits the substrate's shape
the substrate binds anywhere on the enzyme surface
the enzyme is used up in the reaction
explanation: Koshland's model says the active site is flexible and moulds around the substrate, which strains bonds and helps the reaction. A rigid, exactly fitting active site is the older lock-and-key idea, and in both models the enzyme is not used up.

stem: A non-protein organic cofactor that is loosely attached to an enzyme during the reaction is called a
explanation: Coenzymes such as NAD are organic and attach only loosely, so they can move between enzymes. A prosthetic group is also organic but tightly (often covalently) bound, activators are inorganic ions, and the apoenzyme is the protein part itself.

stem: Malonate resembles succinate and slows the enzyme succinate dehydrogenase. Its inhibiting effect can be reduced most effectively by
options: raising the temperature well above optimum
explanation: Malonate is a competitive inhibitor: it competes with succinate for the active site, so adding more substrate makes it more likely that succinate, not malonate, occupies each active site. Heating far above optimum denatures the enzyme, and fewer enzyme molecules or heavy-metal ions only reduce activity further.

stem: A non-competitive inhibitor reduces the rate of an enzyme reaction because it
options: resembles the substrate and occupies the active site
breaks the peptide bonds of the enzyme permanently
binds only to the substrate molecules
binds a site other than the active site and alters the enzyme's shape
explanation: A non-competitive inhibitor attaches to another (allosteric) site, changing the shape of the active site so the substrate cannot be converted; adding more substrate does not overcome it. Occupying the active site because of similar shape is how a competitive inhibitor works.

stem: In an enzyme reaction with a fixed amount of enzyme, the rate stops increasing at high substrate concentration because
options: the enzyme is denatured by excess substrate
all active sites are occupied at any moment
the product is no longer formed
explanation: Once every active site is busy, extra substrate molecules have to wait for a free site, so the rate reaches a maximum and levels off. The enzyme is not denatured by substrate; to raise the rate further, more enzyme is needed.

stem: An enzyme extract with optimum 37 °C is held at 70 °C for 10 minutes and then cooled back to 37 °C. Its activity at 37 °C will be
options: very low, because its active site has been permanently changed
normal, because cooling back to 37 °C restores the original shape
higher than before, because it has been activated
normal, but only after more substrate is added
explanation: High temperature breaks the hydrogen and ionic bonds that hold the active site in shape, so the enzyme is denatured and does not refold on cooling. Low temperatures only inactivate enzymes temporarily, which is why expecting recovery on cooling is the common mistake.
